## The Problem

Your genome has **3 billion base pairs** — a sequence of A, T, G, C.

No machine can read it all at once.

Instead: shred many copies of the genome into millions of short fragments,
read each fragment, and **reassemble**.

This is called **shotgun sequencing**.

::: notes
Shotgun sequencing is the dominant method since the Human Genome Project (2003).
The "shotgun" metaphor: randomly blast the genome into tiny pieces, then figure
out how they fit back together from the overlaps.
:::

## The Fragments Arrive as Data {.smaller}

Each fragment is a short string of bases — a **k-mer**.

For a toy genome and k=3:

```python
import pandas as pd

genome = "ATGCAT"   # pretend it's circular
k = 3

kmers = [genome[i:i+k] for i in range(len(genome))]
df = pd.DataFrame({'kmer': kmers})
```

```
   kmer
0   ATG
1   TGC
2   GCA
3   CAT
```

In real sequencing: millions of rows, k ≈ 100–300.

::: notes
The genome is circular in many organisms (bacteria especially). For simplicity
we start with a circular example — it produces an Euler *circuit* rather than
a path, which is the cleanest case.
:::

## Can You Reassemble It?

Given only this bag of 3-mers — no positions, no order:

```
ATG    TGC    GCA    CAT
```

Can you recover the original sequence?

. . .

*Try it. What do you notice about the fragments?*

::: notes
Give students 30 seconds. They'll notice each fragment overlaps with the next
by k-1 = 2 characters. ATG ends in TG, TGC starts with TG. And so on.
This overlap structure is the key.
:::

## The Overlap Structure

Each k-mer overlaps its neighbours by **k−1** characters.

```
ATG
 TGC
  GCA
   CAT
    AT...
```

The fragments chain together. But with millions of fragments — many of them
identical — you can't just line them up by eye.

We need a systematic approach.

## Naïve Idea: Overlap Graph

Draw a node for each fragment. Draw an edge when two fragments overlap.

```
ATG ──► TGC ──► GCA ──► CAT ──► ATG ...
```

This works! But checking every pair of fragments for overlap costs $O(n^2)$
comparisons. For millions of fragments, that's trillions of checks.

We need a smarter graph.

## A Different Graph {.smaller}

Instead of nodes = k-mers, let **nodes = (k−1)-mers** and **edges = k-mers**.

| k-mer | prefix (k−1) | suffix (k−1) | edge |
|-------|-------------|-------------|------|
| ATG   | AT          | TG          | AT → TG |
| TGC   | TG          | GC          | TG → GC |
| GCA   | GC          | CA          | GC → CA |
| CAT   | CA          | AT          | CA → AT |

Each fragment becomes an **edge** between its prefix and suffix.

::: notes
This is the de Bruijn graph construction. Named after Nicolaas de Bruijn.
The key insight: the overlap structure is captured by the shared (k-1)-mer
between consecutive edges.
:::

## The de Bruijn Graph

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
| k-mer | edge |
|-------|------|
| ATG   | AT → TG |
| TGC   | TG → GC |
| GCA   | GC → CA |
| CAT   | CA → AT |
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{dot}
digraph G {
  rankdir=LR
  node [shape=circle style=filled fillcolor="#4a90d9" fontcolor=white fontsize=14 width=0.6]
  AT -> TG [label="ATG"]
  TG -> GC [label="TGC"]
  GC -> CA [label="GCA"]
  CA -> AT [label="CAT"]
}
```
:::
:::::

Nodes are 2-mers. Edges are 3-mers (our reads).

**The genome is hidden in this graph — but how do we read it out?**

## What Does Traversal Mean Here?

Assembling the genome = spelling out all four reads **in order**.

That means visiting every **edge** exactly once.

. . .

*What kind of graph traversal visits every edge exactly once?*

. . .

## Euler's Circuit {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {style="text-align:center; font-size:1.4em; margin-top: 1.5em"}
**An Euler circuit visits every edge exactly once.**
:::

::: {style="text-align:center; margin-top: 1em; color: #aad4f5"}
Leonhard Euler, 1736 — the Königsberg bridge problem.
:::

::: {style="text-align:center; margin-top: 1.5em; font-size:1.1em"}
Genome assembly **is** finding an Euler circuit in the de Bruijn graph.
:::

::: notes
Euler proved in 1736 that the Königsberg bridge problem (can you cross each of
7 bridges exactly once?) had no solution, by analysing the degree of each
landmass. That paper is widely considered the birth of graph theory.
290 years later, the same idea assembles genomes.
:::

## When Does an Euler Circuit Exist?

**Euler's theorem**: A connected directed graph has an Euler circuit if and only if
every node has equal in-degree and out-degree.

Check our graph:

| Node | Out | In | Balanced? |
|------|-----|----|-----------|
| AT   | 1   | 1  | ✓ |
| TG   | 1   | 1  | ✓ |
| GC   | 1   | 1  | ✓ |
| CA   | 1   | 1  | ✓ |

Assembly is possible.

::: notes
For a linear genome (Euler PATH rather than circuit): exactly one node has
out − in = 1 (start), exactly one has in − out = 1 (end), all others balanced.
Real genomes are linear, so we look for an Euler path. Checking degrees tells
you immediately whether assembly is even possible — before you run any algorithm.
:::

## Euler Path vs. Euler Circuit

| | Circuit | Path |
|---|---|---|
| Start = End? | Yes | No |
| Degree condition | All nodes balanced | Exactly two unbalanced nodes |
| Genome type | Circular (bacteria) | Linear (humans) |

For a linear genome: find the unique node with $\text{out} - \text{in} = 1$. That's your start.

::: notes
This is a beautiful pre-check: before running any algorithm, just compute
in-degrees and out-degrees. O(E). If the condition fails, assembly from these
reads is impossible (there are gaps or errors in your data).
:::

## From Euler to Code

We know **DFS** from week 6. Here is the classic version:

```python
def dfs(graph, v, visited, path):
    visited.add(v)
    path.append(v)          # pre-order: record on arrival
    for w in graph[v]:
        if w not in visited:
            dfs(graph, w, visited, path)
```

This visits each **node** once. We need to visit each **edge** once.

Two things must change — and the second one is subtle.

::: notes
Don't reveal the answer yet — this is the bridge to the code task.
The two changes:
1. Track consumed edges (pop from adjacency list) instead of visited nodes
2. Move path.append to AFTER recursion (post-order)
The second change is what makes the "splicing" work.
:::
